results.result: The RhopH complex is synthesized as a soluble heterotrimeric complex with 1:1:1 stoichiometry of CLAG3, RhopH2, and RhopH3, as determined by native mass spectrometry yielding a molecular weight of 433,790 ± 10 Da. A minor CLAG3–RhopH2 heterodimer was also detected.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C28, and C29 are well-supported by native mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The measured mass matches the expected mass for a 1:1:1 heterotrimeric complex with only 0.6% error, and the detection of a minor heterodimer provides additional validation of the methodology.

results.result: The cryo-EM structure of the RhopH complex was determined at 2.9 Å resolution, revealing that CLAG3 mediates subunit associations through independent contacts with RhopH2 (2005 Å² interface) and RhopH3 (3700 Å² interface), which do not directly interact with each other. CLAG3 contains three distinct domains: an N-terminal sphere, a central bridge for RhopH2 binding, and a C-terminal bundle encasing an amphipathic helix.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C32-C40 are strongly supported by the cryo-EM data presented in Figure 2 and Table 1. The resolution of 2.9 Å is sufficient for confident model building, and the structural features described (domain architecture, interface areas, subunit interactions) are directly observable in the density maps and validated by the refined atomic model.

results.result: The soluble RhopH complex is tightly assembled with extensive intramolecular disulfide bonding within each subunit. No intermolecular disulfide bonds between subunits were detected, though several cysteines were not visualized and could potentially form such interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C41, and C42 are supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2G-H. The observed intramolecular disulfide bonds are clearly identified in the structure, and the authors appropriately note the limitation that some cysteines were not visualized, leaving open the possibility of intermolecular bonding.

results.result: Predicted transmembrane helices are shielded in the soluble RhopH complex. CLAG3 α-helix 44 (the single confidently predicted transmembrane domain) is buried within a C-terminal bundle with hydrophobic Phe residues segregated to one surface and polar residues on the opposite face. The transmembrane domains of RhopH2 and RhopH3 are also buried, with all three helices separated by 46–101 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C47, C50-C54, and C80 are well-supported by structural data in Figure 3. The burial of predicted transmembrane helices is clearly shown, and the segregation of hydrophobic and polar residues on helix 44 is consistent with its proposed role as a pore-lining helix. The quantitative measurements of helix separation are derived from the atomic model.

results.result: Freeze-thaw releases CLAG3 from a peripheral membrane pool, while hypotonic treatment does not release CLAG3. Alkaline Na2CO3 extraction partially releases CLAG3, implicating both integral and peripheral membrane pools.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by biochemical fractionation data shown in Figure 1B. The differential release by these treatments provides evidence for distinct membrane-associated pools of CLAG3, though the mechanism of freeze-thaw release could be further characterized.

results.result: The purified RhopH complex resists aggregation and unfolding at temperatures above those seen in malaria fevers and has a two-lobed structure as determined by 3D reconstruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C30 and C31 are supported by thermal stability assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C) and 3D reconstruction (Figure 1G). The thermal stability data show denaturation above 55°C, which is well above fever temperatures (~40°C), and the two-lobed architecture is consistently observed across multiple imaging approaches.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis reveals that P. falciparum CLAG paralogs cluster into well-supported groups containing species infecting other mammals, while CLAG9 represents an older lineage that clustered independently.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C44 are supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A. The tree topology with bootstrap support values provides evidence for the clustering patterns described, though the evolutionary interpretation could benefit from additional molecular clock or selection analyses.

results.result: Structural similarity searches revealed that RhopH3 exhibits similarity with domains from SepL (a bacterial type III secretion regulator) and RhopH2 partially aligns with Bcl-xL (an anti-apoptotic protein regulating membrane permeabilization).
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C46 are supported by structural similarity searches using the Dali server, with results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B-C. The Z-scores (6.0 for SepL, 4.2 for Bcl-xL) indicate statistically significant structural similarities, though the functional implications remain speculative.

results.result: During schizont-stage synthesis, both peripheral and integral membrane pools of CLAG3 are detected, with the integral pool representing protein from the previous cycle (as shown by protease susceptibility). Purified merozoites contain only carbonate-extractable CLAG3. Through the parasite cycle, CLAG3 transitions from a primarily extractable form in schizonts to a growing integral pool in trophozoites.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are well-supported by stage-dependent fractionation studies shown in Figure 4A-E. The protease susceptibility experiments (Figure 4A-B) provide strong evidence that the integral pool in schizonts represents prior-cycle protein, and the time-course data clearly show the transition from soluble to integral forms.

results.result: The RhopH complex crosses the parasitophorous vacuolar membrane and becomes integral to the erythrocyte membrane through a PTEX translocon-dependent process. PTEX knockdown abolishes CLAG3 transition to an integral form (p = 0.01, n = 3), and CLAG3 that failed to insert was more readily solubilized.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C61, and C62 are supported by PTEX knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4F. The statistical significance (p = 0.01) with n = 3 replicates provides adequate evidence for PTEX-dependent membrane insertion, though the mechanism (direct translocation vs. indirect effects) remains uncertain.

results.result: Protease susceptibility studies show that soluble CLAG3 pools (freeze-thaw released and carbonate-extractable) are unaffected by extracellular protease, while the integral pool yields a C-terminal cleavage product that remains membrane embedded. CLAG3 α-helix 44 is within this protease-resistant fragment and likely provides the transmembrane anchor.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by protease susceptibility data in Figure 4G. The differential protease sensitivity of soluble vs. integral pools provides strong evidence for membrane topology, and the inference that helix 44 provides the transmembrane anchor is reasonable based on its location within the protease-resistant fragment.

results.result: The authors propose that the RhopH complex undergoes large-scale rearrangements for host membrane insertion, paralleling smaller two-state pore-forming proteins. The complex evolved as a modular three-protein assembly suited for divergent functions at separate points in the parasite cycle, with a soluble form facilitating RhopH3 contribution to invasion.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C66, C67, and C81 represent proposals and inferences based on the structural and biochemical data. While the shielding of transmembrane helices and their spatial separation (46-101 Å) in the soluble structure strongly suggest large-scale rearrangements are required, direct evidence of these conformational changes is lacking. The parallel to two-state pore-forming proteins is speculative.

results.result: Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved A1215 in CLAG3 transmembrane domain alters channel properties, and CLAG3 α-helix 44 and neighboring helices align significantly with APH-1, an integral membrane component of human γ-secretase.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C49 are supported by cited prior work (Sharma et al., 2015) and structural similarity searches (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The mutagenesis data from the cited work provides functional validation for helix 44's role in channel function, and the structural alignment with APH-1 supports its membrane-spanning nature.

results.result: RhopH3 has a large exposed surface area of ~32,000 Å². Structural similarity searches found that RhopH3 residues 434-665 align with domains 2 and 3 of SepL, and the RhopH3 C-terminus (residues 716-897) is not resolved in the structure and appears flexible.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by structural analysis and similarity searches. The surface area calculation is derived from the atomic model, the SepL alignment is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, and the lack of density for the C-terminus is evident in the structure. However, the speculation about receptor interaction at the SepL-aligned site lacks experimental validation.

results.result: The soluble RhopH complex is deposited in the parasitophorous vacuole in a soluble form. RhopH subunits may be exported into host cell cytosol via PTEX, and the complex may directly interact with PTEX. However, PTEX appears to lack a lateral gate, and the authors favor membrane insertion after transfer into host cytosol.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 mix established findings (C71 is supported by fractionation data) with cited suggestions (C72-C74) and author speculation (C75). While the PTEX-dependence of membrane insertion is established (C61), the precise mechanism—whether insertion occurs during or after PTEX translocation—remains unresolved. The lack of a lateral gate in PTEX is cited but does not definitively rule out co-translational insertion.

results.result: Various studies support a role of the RhopH complex in PSAC formation and nutrient uptake. Prior in vitro selection implicated a CLAG3 amphipathic motif in channel selectivity and gating. CLAG3 oligomerizes at the host membrane with a surface-exposed variant region, while RhopH2 and RhopH3 are not exposed based on protease susceptibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by multiple cited studies. These claims represent established knowledge from prior work rather than new findings from this study. The protease susceptibility data for RhopH2 and RhopH3 (Ito et al., 2017) and CLAG3 oligomerization studies (Gupta et al., 2018) provide the evidence base.

results.result: The RhopH complex contributes to multiple essential functions in the malaria parasite lifecycle: RhopH3 facilitates erythrocyte invasion, and CLAG3 (along with RhopH2 and RhopH3) forms the PSAC channel for nutrient uptake approximately 18 hours after invasion.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C14, C22-C24 represent established knowledge from prior studies (cited throughout the introduction). While these are not new findings from this manuscript, they provide the essential context for the structural and mechanistic studies presented. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: The RhopH complex subunits (CLAG, RhopH2, and RhopH3) are conserved and restricted to Plasmodium spp. with no significant homology to proteins in other genera. RhopH2 and RhopH3 are single-copy genes, while CLAG proteins are encoded by a multigene family with variable expansion across malaria parasite species.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C15-C19 represent established knowledge from prior studies (cited in the introduction). These claims are well-supported by the cited literature and provide important context for understanding the uniqueness of the RhopH complex and the challenges in studying it.

results.result: Malaria parasites evade host immunity by replicating within vertebrate erythrocytes. P. falciparum uses multiple ligands for erythrocyte invasion and remodels its host cell to achieve tissue adherence and nutrient acquisition.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 represent well-established background knowledge about malaria parasite biology, supported by the cited literature. These provide essential context but are not new findings from this study.

results.result: RhopH subunits are transcribed in mature schizont-infected erythrocytes and assemble into a complex that is packaged into rhoptry organelles. During conversion to integral form, CLAG3 remains associated with other RhopH subunits.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C21, and C60 are supported by cited prior work (Ling et al., 2004; Ito et al., 2017) and data from this study (Figure 1A for C20, cited work for C21, and cited work for C60). The association of subunits during membrane insertion is an important finding that constrains models of the insertion mechanism.
